title: CT Scans of Rare Dodo Skulls Uncover a Sensory World We Never Knew
summary:
For centuries, the dodo has been the poster child for extinction and, unfairly, for stupidity. But new research using cutting-edge CT scans on the world's only two complete dodo skulls is flipping that narrative. Scientists have digitally reconstructed the dodo's brain cavity and uncovered evidence of a surprisingly sophisticated sensory system.

The study, published in the Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, focused on a rare skull housed at the Natural History Museum Denmark. Preparations for a new museum building gave researchers an unprecedented chance to scan the specimen in high resolution. "Studying extinct animals is a bit like detective work," said co-author Christy Anna Hipsley. "Although the dodo's brain disappeared centuries ago, it left an imprint on the inside of the skull."

By comparing these digital brain models to those of modern pigeons and doves, the team identified several crucial differences. The dodo's olfactory bulbs—the brain regions for smell—were enlarged, suggesting a stronger reliance on scent for finding food. Its large upper beak was likely packed with tactile nerves, making it a sensitive tool for probing the ground. Furthermore, the anatomy hints that the dodo may have been active not just during the day, but also around dawn and dusk, a more flexible schedule than its relatives.

"The dodo's skull is unlike that of any living bird, which makes it both fascinating and difficult to interpret," Hipsley added. The findings challenge the popular image of a clumsy, dim-witted bird. Instead, the dodo appears to have been well-adapted to its isolated island habitat on Mauritius, with a unique set of sensory skills honed over millions of years. While the study can't reveal exact behavior, it provides a much-needed evidence-based framework for understanding how this iconic bird truly lived before its extinction in the late 17th century. As co-author Peter Andrew Hosner put it, "Every new piece of evidence helps us move beyond myths and build a more accurate picture of how this extraordinary bird lived before it disappeared."
why_it_matters: The dodo’s story shows how science can correct outdated stereotypes, reminding us that extinction is an irreversible loss of unique adaptations — a lesson relevant as human actions continue to threaten species today.

background_read: The dodo, a flightless bird that lived only on the island of Mauritius (a small island nation in the Indian Ocean), was driven to extinction by the late 1600s—less than a century after humans arrived.
Today only a handful of bones and two complete skulls remain, making any new study a rare chance to learn about its life.
The research used CT scanning, a technique originally developed for medical imaging in the 1970s, to peer inside the fragile fossils without damaging them.
The study was published in the journal of the Linnean Society (a scientific association founded in London in 1788 that focuses on natural history and taxonomy).
Previous views of the dodo as clumsy came from early sailors’ accounts and illustrations, but modern science is now painting a more accurate picture.

perspectives.description: Scientists and conservationists gain a more accurate understanding of extinct species, which can improve conservation strategies for living birds that face similar island pressures.

The early myth that the dodo was stupid created a false narrative that hid its true ecological role; such biases can still shape public perception of extinction and downplay the urgency of protecting endangered animals.

The study illustrates how technological advances like CT scanning open windows into the past by revealing anatomy without destroying rare fossils. This is a recurring pattern in paleontology: new tools constantly reshape what we think we know about extinct life.

Future research on other dodo skull fragments or ancient DNA could uncover even more details about its behaviour and senses. Together with ecological modelling, scientists might eventually reconstruct the lost world of Mauritius and better understand how species adapt to isolated environments.
